I can prepare primary and secondary amines from halogenoalkanes and reduce nitriles/amides.
I can prepare phenylamine and describe bromination, diazotisation and azo coupling.
I can write the formation, hydrolysis and reduction equations for amides.
I can explain why amides are weaker bases than amines.
I can draw amino acid forms, zwitterions and peptide bonds.
I can use isoelectric points and electrophoresis results to infer charge and relative size.

title: 34 Nitrogen compounds
34 Nitrogen compounds
text:
An amine contains a nitrogen atom with a lone pair. A primary amine has one carbon-containing group attached to nitrogen, while a secondary amine has two:
\[RNH₂ \qquad \text{primary amine}\]
\[R₂NH \qquad \text{secondary amine}\]
The lone pair makes amines Brønsted–Lowry bases: they accept a proton by forming a dative covalent bond to H⁺.
\[RNH₂ + H₂O ⇌ RNH₃⁺ + OH⁻\]
\[RNH₂ + HCl → RNH₃⁺Cl⁻\]
Alkyl groups have a positive inductive effect and push electron density towards nitrogen. This generally makes an aliphatic secondary amine more basic than ammonia. In phenylamine, the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton. A typical order is:
\[\text{phenylamine} < \text{ammonia} < \text{primary amine} < \text{secondary amine}\]



Structures of ammonia, phenylamine and an aliphatic secondary amine





Relative basicity of amines




Worked example · Comparing amine basicity


Explain why phenylamine is a weaker base than ammonia, whereas an aliphatic secondary amine is a stronger base than ammonia.


Base strength depends on the availability of the lone pair on nitrogen to accept H⁺.
In phenylamine, the nitrogen lone pair overlaps with the benzene ring and is delocalised into the ring. It is therefore less available to accept a proton.
Alkyl groups have a positive inductive effect and push electron density towards nitrogen.
In an aliphatic secondary amine, two alkyl groups increase the electron density on nitrogen, making the lone pair more available.
Therefore phenylamine is less basic than ammonia, while an aliphatic secondary amine is more basic than ammonia.






Halogenoalkanes react with ammonia by nucleophilic substitution. Use excess ethanolic ammonia, heat and pressure in a sealed tube. Excess ammonia reduces further reaction of the primary amine product:
\[CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br\]
A primary amine can also react with a halogenoalkane to give a secondary amine:
\[RBr + R'NH₂ → R–NHR' + HBr\]



Preparation of amines from halogenoalkanes




Worked example · Preparing an amine


State the reagents and conditions required for the conversion of 1-bromobutane into butylamine.


Use excess ammonia, NH₃.
Use ethanol as the solvent.
Heat the mixture under pressure, usually in a sealed tube.
The reaction is nucleophilic substitution, replacing bromine with NH₂.






Amides are reduced to amines using lithium aluminium hydride, LiAlH₄, usually in dry ether followed by hydrolysis. An N-substituted amide gives a secondary amine:
\[RCONH₂ → RCH₂NH₂ + H₂O\]
\[RCONHR' → RCH₂NHR' + H₂O\]
Nitriles can be reduced to primary amines using LiAlH₄ in dry ether or H₂ with a nickel catalyst:
\[RCN + 2H₂ → RCH₂NH₂\]



Reduction of an amide to an amine





Reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine




Worked example · Reducing an amide


N-methylpropanamide can undergo reduction forming compound Y and water. State the reagent required and identify the type of amine formed.


Use lithium aluminium hydride, LiAlH₄, in dry ether, followed by hydrolysis.
The carbonyl group CONH is reduced to CH₂NH.
Because the nitrogen remains attached to a methyl group and an alkyl chain, compound Y is a secondary amine.






Ammonia and primary amines react with acyl chlorides by nucleophilic addition–elimination. The nitrogen lone pair attacks the electron-deficient carbonyl carbon, chloride is eliminated and the carbonyl group reforms. A second molecule of ammonia or amine neutralises the hydrogen chloride formed:
\[RCOCl + 2NH₃ → RCONH₂ + NH₄Cl\]
\[RCOCl + 2R'NH₂ → RCONHR' + R'NH₃Cl\]
For example:
\[CH₃COCl + 2CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₃ + CH₃NH₃Cl\]



Reaction of acyl chlorides with ammonia and amines

title: 34 Nitrogen compounds
text:
Phenylamine, C₆H₅NH₂, is prepared from nitrobenzene by reduction. The syllabus method uses tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, with heat, followed by aqueous sodium hydroxide to liberate the free amine:
\[C₆H₅NO₂ → C₆H₅NH₃⁺Cl⁻ → C₆H₅NH₂\]
Hydrogen with a nickel, platinum or palladium catalyst, or LiAlH₄ in dry ether, are also suitable reducing systems.
Phenylamine reacts readily with bromine water because the NH₂ group activates the benzene ring and directs substitution to the 2-, 4- and 6-positions:
\[C₆H₅NH₂ + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃NH₂ + 3HBr\]



Reduction of nitrobenzene to phenylamine





Bromination of phenylamine




Worked example · Phenylamine synthesis


Name the type of reaction and suggest suitable reagents and conditions for the conversion of nitrobenzene into phenylamine.


The reaction is a reduction.
Heat nitrobenzene with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid.
Add aqueous sodium hydroxide after the reduction to release phenylamine from its salt.
An alternative is H₂ with a nickel catalyst, or LiAlH₄ in dry ether.






Phenylamine reacts with nitrous acid below 10 °C to form a diazonium salt. Nitrous acid is made in situ from sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid:
\[NaNO₂ + HCl → HNO₂ + NaCl\]
\[C₆H₅NH₂ + HCl + HNO₂ → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + 2H₂O\]

The diazonium ion acts as an electrophile and couples with a phenol or phenoxide ion. Coupling usually occurs at the position para to the hydroxyl group. The product contains the azo group, –N=N–, which extends conjugation between aromatic rings and gives intensely coloured azo dyes.
\[C₆H₅N₂⁺ + C₆H₅O⁻ → C₆H₅–N=N–C₆H₄–OH\]



Azo coupling with phenol





Azo dye synthesis




Worked example · Stabilising a diazonium salt


Phenylamine is converted into a diazonium salt before it is coupled with an alkaline phenol solution. State a condition that prevents the diazonium salt from decomposing and explain the role of the azo group in the dye.


Keep the reaction mixture ice-cold, or below 10 °C.
The low temperature prevents the unstable diazonium salt from decomposing.
The diazonium ion is an electrophile and reacts with the electron-rich phenoxide ring.
The product contains –N=N–, the azo group, which connects two aromatic systems.
The extended delocalised system absorbs visible light, so the azo compound is strongly coloured.

title: 36 Organic synthesis
text:
本章对应 CIE 9701 2025–2027 syllabus 的 36.1 Organic synthesis。题目部分对应专题题包 7.8 Organic Synthesis (A Level Only)；完整 Easy、Medium、Hard Structured Questions 放在本页底部的 Structured Questions 页面。


学完本节后，你应该能够：

identify functional groups in molecules containing more than one functional group;
predict the properties and reactions of molecules containing several functional groups;
devise a multi-step synthetic route to a target molecule;
analyse a synthetic route by identifying the reaction type, reagents and conditions, and possible by-products;
choose a route with appropriate selectivity, atom economy and separation requirements.






When a molecule contains several functional groups, identify each group independently before predicting its reactions. The same molecule may contain an arene, an alkene, an alcohol, a phenol, an amine, a carbonyl group, a carboxylic acid, an ester, an amide or a nitrile.
The functional group controls the characteristic reaction, while the other groups may alter the rate or position of reaction. For example, a phenolic \(-\)OH group activates the 2-, 4- and 6-positions of an aromatic ring, whereas a \(-\)COOH or \(-\)COCl group is electron-withdrawing and directs electrophilic substitution mainly to the 3- and 5-positions.



Functional groups in molecules containing more than one functional group





Alkyl side chains attached to an aromatic ring can be oxidised completely to a carboxylic acid using hot alkaline potassium manganate(VII), followed by acidification. The carbon attached directly to the ring must have at least one hydrogen atom for this oxidation to occur.
\[\ce{Ar-CH3 ->[KMnO4(aq), OH-, heat][H+] Ar-COOH}\]
Benzoic acid is therefore a useful intermediate in a synthesis. Its carboxylic acid group is electron-withdrawing and directs later electrophilic substitution to the meta position.



Preparation and reactions of benzoic acid





Acyl chlorides are very reactive derivatives of carboxylic acids. They undergo nucleophilic addition–elimination with water, alcohols, ammonia and amines.
\[\ce{RCOCl + H2O -> RCOOH + HCl}\]
\[\ce{RCOCl + R'OH -> RCOOR' + HCl}\]
\[\ce{RCOCl + 2R'NH2 -> RCONHR' + R'NH3Cl}\]
An acyl chloride can be made from a carboxylic acid using thionyl chloride, \(\ce{SOCl2}\), or phosphorus pentachloride. The reaction is useful in synthesis because it is rapid and usually gives a higher yield than direct esterification.



Reactions of acyl chlorides





Formation and reactions of amides





In electrophilic aromatic substitution, an electrophile attacks the delocalised \(\pi\) system of an aromatic ring. A temporary positively charged intermediate forms, then loss of \(\ce{H+}\) restores the delocalised ring.
For a Friedel–Crafts acylation:
\[\ce{CH3COCl + AlCl3 -> CH3CO+ + AlCl4-}\]
The acylium ion, \(\ce{CH3CO+}\), is the electrophile. The catalyst is regenerated when the intermediate loses a proton.
Electron-donating groups such as \(\ce{-CH3}\) and \(\ce{-OH}\) activate the 2-, 4- and 6-positions. Electron-withdrawing groups such as \(\ce{-COOH}\), \(\ce{-COCl}\) and \(\ce{-NO2}\) deactivate the ring and direct substitution mainly to the 3- and 5-positions.



Electrophilic substitution of arenes





Hydrogenation of benzene




Worked example · Designing a multi-step synthesis


Suggest how the following synthesis could be carried out:
Ethene to 1-aminopropane


Add HCl to ethene at room temperature to form chloroethane by electrophilic addition:
\[\ce{CH2=CH2 + HCl -> CH3CH2Cl}\]
Heat chloroethane under reflux with ethanolic KCN or NaCN. Nucleophilic substitution adds one carbon atom and forms propanenitrile:
\[\ce{CH3CH2Cl + CN- -> CH3CH2CN + Cl-}\]
Reduce propanenitrile using \(\ce{LiAlH4}\) in dry ether, followed by hydrolysis, to form 1-aminopropane:
\[\ce{CH3CH2CN + 2H2 ->[LiAlH4] CH3CH2CH2NH2}\]

The route uses three different transformations: electrophilic addition, nucleophilic substitution and reduction of a nitrile.





Phenol is less reactive than an aliphatic alcohol in some reactions, but its aromatic ring is strongly activated by the \(\ce{-OH}\) group. Phenol reacts with acyl chlorides to form phenyl esters:
\[\ce{C6H5OH + CH3COCl -> C6H5OCOCH3 + HCl}\]
It is a weak acid. It reacts with sodium hydroxide to form sodium phenoxide, but it is not sufficiently acidic to react appreciably with aqueous sodium carbonate:
\[\ce{C6H5OH + NaOH -> C6H5ONa + H2O}\]
The activated ring undergoes bromination readily, often producing a 2,4,6-tribromophenol precipitate, and nitration can occur under milder conditions than for benzene.



Esterification of phenol





Acid-base reactions of phenol





Nitration and bromination of phenol





Common transformations that extend or modify an aliphatic carbon chain include:

alkene + \(\ce{HCl}\) or \(\ce{HBr}\): electrophilic addition to form a halogenoalkane;
halogenoalkane + aqueous \(\ce{OH-}\): nucleophilic substitution to form an alcohol;
halogenoalkane + ethanolic \(\ce{CN-}\): nucleophilic substitution that increases the carbon chain by one carbon;
primary alcohol + acidified dichromate(VI), distil: oxidation to an aldehyde;
aldehyde + acidified dichromate(VI), reflux: oxidation to a carboxylic acid;
ketone or carboxylic acid + \(\ce{LiAlH4}\): reduction;
nitrile + \(\ce{LiAlH4}\): reduction to a primary amine.

The reagent, solvent, temperature and method of isolation must all be specified. For example, distillation removes an aldehyde as it forms, whereas reflux allows further oxidation to a carboxylic acid.



Aliphatic reaction pathways





An aromatic synthesis should be planned backwards from the target. Identify the last functional-group change first, then select an earlier intermediate that can be converted selectively.
Useful sequences include:
\[\ce{benzene ->[conc. HNO3/H2SO4] nitrobenzene ->[Sn/HCl, heat] phenylamine}\]
\[\ce{benzene ->[RCl/AlCl3] alkylbenzene ->[KMnO4, reflux][H+] benzoic\ acid}\]
\[\ce{benzene ->[RCOCl/AlCl3] aryl\ ketone ->[NaBH4] secondary\ alcohol}\]
The order matters. A methyl group activates the 2-, 4- and 6-positions, while a carbonyl-containing group such as \(\ce{-COCl}\) directs substitution meta. A shorter route is not automatically better if it gives the wrong isomer or a mixture that is difficult to separate.



Aromatic reaction pathways




Worked example · Analysis of synthetic routes


Some reactions of compound A are shown below.
1. Give the structure of compound B and state the type of reaction by which this compound is formed from compound A.
2. What are the suitable reagents for reaction 2?
3. Suggest a more effective way to synthesise compound D from compound A.
4. What are the possible by-products of reaction 4?


Reaction 1 is hydrogenation of the aromatic ring. Compound B is the corresponding cyclohexane derivative. The reaction is reduction (addition of hydrogen).
Oxidise the alkyl side chain using hot alkaline \(\ce{KMnO4}\) under reflux, then acidify with dilute sulfuric acid. The side chain is converted into a carboxylic acid.
A more effective route is to convert the carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride using \(\ce{SOCl2}\), then react the acyl chloride with the alcohol. This is faster and more complete than direct esterification with the carboxylic acid.
The acyl-chloride esterification produces hydrogen chloride, HCl. If direct esterification is used, the possible by-product is water, H\(_2\)O. Any unreacted starting material or hydrolysis product may also require separation.

The key route-analysis questions are: what bond changes, which reagent performs that change, what conditions give the desired selectivity, and what additional substances must be removed afterwards.





For a proposed route, analyse every arrow using four questions:

What reaction type occurs? For example, oxidation, reduction, nucleophilic substitution, electrophilic substitution, esterification or hydrolysis.
Which reagent is required? Give the actual laboratory reagent, not only the reactive ion.
What conditions are needed? Include solvent, catalyst, temperature, pressure, reflux or distillation where relevant.
What can go wrong? Consider competing products, regioisomers, over-oxidation, incomplete reaction, hydrolysis, low atom economy and difficult separation.




A multi-step synthesis example


The best route is usually one that gives the correct isomer in a small number of selective steps, uses readily available reagents, minimises waste and avoids difficult separations. A route with fewer arrows is not necessarily better if one step gives the wrong directing effect or a mixture of products.



Analysis of a synthetic route





Possible by-products in a synthetic route







I can identify every functional group in a molecule containing several functional groups.
I can predict how electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups affect aromatic substitution.
I can select reagents and conditions for oxidation, reduction, substitution, addition, esterification and hydrolysis.
I can add one carbon to an aliphatic chain using a nitrile intermediate.
I can design a multi-step route by working backwards from a target molecule.
I can analyse by-products, competing reactions and separation requirements.

\[\ce{RCOCl + 2R'NH2 -> RCONHR' + R'NH3Cl}\]
An acyl chloride can be made from a carboxylic acid using thionyl chloride, \(\ce{SOCl2}\), or phosphorus pentachloride. The reaction is useful in synthesis because it is rapid and usually gives a higher yield than direct esterification.



Reactions of acyl chlorides





Formation and reactions of amides





In electrophilic aromatic substitution, an electrophile attacks the delocalised \(\pi\) system of an aromatic ring. A temporary positively charged intermediate forms, then loss of \(\ce{H+}\) restores the delocalised ring.
For a Friedel–Crafts acylation:
\[\ce{CH3COCl + AlCl3 -> CH3CO+ + AlCl4-}\]
The acylium ion, \(\ce{CH3CO+}\), is the electrophile. The catalyst is regenerated when the intermediate loses a proton.
Electron-donating groups such as \(\ce{-CH3}\) and \(\ce{-OH}\) activate the 2-, 4- and 6-positions. Electron-withdrawing groups such as \(\ce{-COOH}\), \(\ce{-COCl}\) and \(\ce{-NO2}\) deactivate the ring and direct substitution mainly to the 3- and 5-positions.



Electrophilic substitution of arenes





Hydrogenation of benzene




Worked example · Designing a multi-step synthesis


Suggest how the following synthesis could be carried out:
Ethene to 1-aminopropane


Add HCl to ethene at room temperature to form chloroethane by electrophilic addition:
\[\ce{CH2=CH2 + HCl -> CH3CH2Cl}\]
Heat chloroethane under reflux with ethanolic KCN or NaCN. Nucleophilic substitution adds one carbon atom and forms propanenitrile:
\[\ce{CH3CH2Cl + CN- -> CH3CH2CN + Cl-}\]
Reduce propanenitrile using \(\ce{LiAlH4}\) in dry ether, followed by hydrolysis, to form 1-aminopropane:
\[\ce{CH3CH2CN + 2H2 ->[LiAlH4] CH3CH2CH2NH2}\]

The route uses three different transformations: electrophilic addition, nucleophilic substitution and reduction of a nitrile.





Phenol is less reactive than an aliphatic alcohol in some reactions, but its aromatic ring is strongly activated by the \(\ce{-OH}\) group. Phenol reacts with acyl chlorides to form phenyl esters:
\[\ce{C6H5OH + CH3COCl -> C6H5OCOCH3 + HCl}\]
It is a weak acid. It reacts with sodium hydroxide to form sodium phenoxide, but it is not sufficiently acidic to react appreciably with aqueous sodium carbonate:
\[\ce{C6H5OH + NaOH -> C6H5ONa + H2O}\]
The activated ring undergoes bromination readily, often producing a 2,4,6-tribromophenol precipitate, and nitration can occur under milder conditions than for benzene.



Esterification of phenol





Acid-base reactions of phenol





Nitration and bromination of phenol





Common transformations that extend or modify an aliphatic carbon chain include:

alkene + \(\ce{HCl}\) or \(\ce{HBr}\): electrophilic addition to form a halogenoalkane;
halogenoalkane + aqueous \(\ce{OH-}\): nucleophilic substitution to form an alcohol;
halogenoalkane + ethanolic \(\ce{CN-}\): nucleophilic substitution that increases the carbon chain by one carbon;
primary alcohol + acidified dichromate(VI), distil: oxidation to an aldehyde;
aldehyde + acidified dichromate(VI), reflux: oxidation to a carboxylic acid;
ketone or carboxylic acid + \(\ce{LiAlH4}\): reduction;
nitrile + \(\ce{LiAlH4}\): reduction to a primary amine.

The reagent, solvent, temperature and method of isolation must all be specified. For example, distillation removes an aldehyde as it forms, whereas reflux allows further oxidation to a carboxylic acid.



Aliphatic reaction pathways





An aromatic synthesis should be planned backwards from the target. Identify the last functional-group change first, then select an earlier intermediate that can be converted selectively.
Useful sequences include:
\[\ce{benzene ->[conc. HNO3/H2SO4] nitrobenzene ->[Sn/HCl, heat] phenylamine}\]
\[\ce{benzene ->[RCl/AlCl3] alkylbenzene ->[KMnO4, reflux][H+] benzoic\ acid}\]
\[\ce{benzene ->[RCOCl/AlCl3] aryl\ ketone ->[NaBH4] secondary\ alcohol}\]
The order matters. A methyl group activates the 2-, 4- and 6-positions, while a carbonyl-containing group such as \(\ce{-COCl}\) directs substitution meta. A shorter route is not automatically better if it gives the wrong isomer or a mixture that is difficult to separate.



Aromatic reaction pathways




Worked example · Analysis of synthetic routes


Some reactions of compound A are shown below.
1. Give the structure of compound B and state the type of reaction by which this compound is formed from compound A.
2. What are the suitable reagents for reaction 2?
3. Suggest a more effective way to synthesise compound D from compound A.
4. What are the possible by-products of reaction 4?


Reaction 1 is hydrogenation of the aromatic ring. Compound B is the corresponding cyclohexane derivative. The reaction is reduction (addition of hydrogen).
Oxidise the alkyl side chain using hot alkaline \(\ce{KMnO4}\) under reflux, then acidify with dilute sulfuric acid. The side chain is converted into a carboxylic acid.
A more effective route is to convert the carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride using \(\ce{SOCl2}\), then react the acyl chloride with the alcohol. This is faster and more complete than direct esterification with the carboxylic acid.
The acyl-chloride esterification produces hydrogen chloride, HCl. If direct esterification is used, the possible by-product is water, H\(_2\)O. Any unreacted starting material or hydrolysis product may also require separation.

The key route-analysis questions are: what bond changes, which reagent performs that change, what conditions give the desired selectivity, and what additional substances must be removed afterwards.





For a proposed route, analyse every arrow using four questions:

What reaction type occurs? For example, oxidation, reduction, nucleophilic substitution, electrophilic substitution, esterification or hydrolysis.
Which reagent is required? Give the actual laboratory reagent, not only the reactive ion.
What conditions are needed? Include solvent, catalyst, temperature, pressure, reflux or distillation where relevant.
What can go wrong? Consider competing products, regioisomers, over-oxidation, incomplete reaction, hydrolysis, low atom economy and difficult separation.




A multi-step synthesis example


The best route is usually one that gives the correct isomer in a small number of selective steps, uses readily available reagents, minimises waste and avoids difficult separations. A route with fewer arrows is not necessarily better if one step gives the wrong directing effect or a mixture of products.
